description: Ismaili Shia dynasty ruling from Cairo (909–1171) that contested Abbasid caliphal legitimacy across the Islamic world; at its height controlled Egypt, Syria, the Hejaz, and North Africa, while its administrative sophistication, religious tolerance, and Cairo's commercial wealth made it a formidable power until Saladin's Sunni restoration.

temporal.notes: Shia Ismaili dynasty; rival caliphate to Abbasids; ended by Saladin who restored Sunni rule

lifecycle_phases.description: Established in Ifriqiya (Tunisia); created new capital Mahdia; extended control over North Africa and Sicily
Conquered Egypt (969); founded Cairo; al-Azhar mosque and university established; controlled Red Sea trade; rivaled Abbasids
Succession crisis; Crusaders arrive and contest Syria; Seljuk pressure; Saladin appointed vizier and abolishes Fatimid caliphate

rise_factors.description: Control of Mediterranean and Red Sea trade made Cairo the wealthiest city in the medieval world
Claimed descent from Fatima (daughter of Muhammad), challenging Abbasid religious legitimacy with a rival Shia caliphate
Cairo's twin city Fustat controlled the Nile-Red Sea route to the Indian Ocean. Fatimid merchants dominated the spice and textile trade between Asia and the Mediterranean for over a century.
The Ismaili da'wa (missionary network) built a transnational support base stretching from North Africa to Iraq and Persia, providing both revenue and intelligence well before the conquest of Egypt.
Fatimid armies drew on Berber, Sudanese, and Armenian mercenaries organized in specialized corps, giving the caliphate military flexibility superior to most contemporaries in the 10th–11th centuries.

decline_factors.description: 1094 succession split created the Nizari-Musta'li schism; effective power passed to viziers while caliphs became figureheads
Crusaders took Jerusalem (1099) and cut off Syrian revenues; Seljuk pressure from northeast; Saladin's Sunni restoration

After al-Mustansir's reign, real power shifted to competing military viziers, Armenian, Sudanese, and Turkish factions repeatedly fought for control, leaving caliphs as figureheads and bleeding the treasury.

The First Crusade's capture of Syrian and Palestinian ports (1099–1124) severed Fatimid commercial access to the Levantine coast, diverting Indian Ocean trade revenue to Crusader and later Genoese merchants.
Egypt's overwhelmingly Sunni population never accepted Ismaili Shiism. The Fatimid reliance on non-Muslim and non-Sunni troops increased this alienation, making mass support mobilization impossible.
